Algorithm 1 describes the proposed Voronoi-based method to solve the open-loop terminal time problem. Given a sample set _WK_ with _K_ random samples directly drawn from ( _ηw_ )<sup>_N_</sup> , one can construct _φ_ ( _WK_ ) and find its optimal _K_<sup>ˆ</sup> seeds. The _k_ -means method can be used to find the seeds of a Voronoi partition as explained in Section 2.4. In addition, in order to determine the number of required seeds, WSS can be used as a measure of variability of points in a cluster. A smaller WSS implies more compact clusters which reduces the size of defined buffers _ε_<sup>(1)</sup> _, · · · , ε_<sup>( ˆ</sup> _K_ ) and the average number of samples in each cell. Note that by increasing _K_<sup>ˆ</sup> , clusters become smaller and the precision of Problem 3 grows. However, eventually, the improvement precision is insignificant compared to the imposed computational complexity. Therefore, we compute WSS as a function of _K_<sup>ˆ</sup> , to explore this trade-off. We propose that the “knee” of the curve provides an efficient compromise between precision and computational complexity. It is shown experimentally in the next section that the knee of WSS vs. _K_<sup>ˆ</sup> curve can be a good representative of the knee on the _p_ ˆ vs. _K_<sup>ˆ</sup> . As a result, _K_<sup>ˆ</sup> can be computed and selected in advance.
